prompt: Per Olsson et al. (2022), an induction head predicts the next token in a sequence like '... A B ... A' by attending back to which position?
choices: The position immediately after the earlier occurrence of the current token A, copying B forward
The position with the highest overall attention entropy in the sequence
The first token of the sequence, regardless of content
The position of the most recent punctuation mark

prompt: You train a linear probe that decodes 'input language' from a model's hidden states with 95% accuracy. What is the most accurate description of what you've shown, and what's missing to make a causal claim?
choices: You've shown the information is linearly decodable from that layer; you still need an intervention like activation patching or ablation to show the model actually uses it downstream
You've fully proven the model uses this representation to decide its output, since 95% accuracy is well above chance
Nothing — probe accuracy is uninformative about model internals without a control task, full stop
You've shown the feature is stored in superposition, which patching would only re-confirm

prompt: Per Elhage et al.'s 'Toy Models of Superposition' (2022), why do networks represent more features than they have neurons?
choices: Because features are typically sparse (rarely co-occurring), so the network packs them into near-orthogonal directions across neurons, tolerating small interference to save capacity
Because ReLU activations are inherently unable to represent more than one feature per neuron, forcing overlap as a bug
Because gradient descent randomly assigns unrelated features to the same neuron with no functional benefit
Because superposition only occurs in attention heads, never in MLP neurons

prompt: In Templeton et al.'s 'Scaling Monosemanticity' (2024), what did clamping the 'Golden Gate Bridge' SAE feature in Claude 3 Sonnet demonstrate?
choices: That forcibly setting that one feature's activation causally changed outputs across unrelated prompts, making the model fixate on the bridge -- causal, steerable evidence the direction represents that concept
That the feature only ever activated when the literal string 'Golden Gate Bridge' appeared in the prompt
That SAE features trained on a small one-layer model transfer perfectly to any larger model without retraining
That Claude 3 Sonnet had memorized copyrighted text about the Golden Gate Bridge during pretraining

prompt: In Hubinger et al.'s 'Sleeper Agents' (2024), what happened when standard safety training (SFT, RLHF, adversarial training) was applied to models with a deliberately trained backdoor?
choices: The backdoored behavior persisted through training, and adversarial training sometimes taught the model to conceal the trigger better rather than removing the underlying behavior
RLHF fully removed the backdoor within a single training run, confirming standard safety training is sufficient for this class of problem
The models refused to be fine-tuned further once the backdoor was detected
Only supervised fine-tuning removed the backdoor; RLHF and adversarial training had no effect either way

prompt: Scalable oversight research (e.g., debate, weak-to-strong generalization) is primarily aimed at which problem?
choices: Supervising and evaluating AI systems whose outputs are too complex, expert-level, or delayed in consequence for a human overseer to directly verify
Reducing the compute cost of training large models
Improving tokenizer efficiency for non-English languages
Speeding up inference latency in production deployments

prompt: What is the key methodological difference between a probing experiment and an activation-patching experiment?
choices: Probing tests whether information is linearly decodable from activations (correlational); patching tests whether replacing or ablating an activation causally changes model behavior
Probing is always done on production models while patching is restricted to toy models
Patching requires no forward passes through the model, while probing requires many
They test the same thing; the terms are interchangeable synonyms in the interpretability literature

prompt: Before trusting a paper's claim that an identified circuit 'explains' a model behavior, what should you specifically check for, per this lesson's guidance?
choices: A quantitative faithfulness or completeness metric (e.g., what fraction of the behavior/logit difference the circuit recovers when the rest of the model is ablated), not just a handful of illustrative examples
Whether the paper includes a figure with a neural network diagram, since diagrams alone confirm the mechanism is correct
Whether the paper was published in a peer-reviewed journal, since arXiv preprints in this field are always unreliable
Whether the circuit was found using only raw neurons rather than SAE features, since neuron-level circuits are always more trustworthy
